articles.title: MAHA suffered heavy losses in the 2026 midterms, but the movement is far from dead
articles.author: Robert Brehm, PhD Candidate in Politics, University of Virginia
paras: Candidates tied to the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement suffered a series of electoral defeats in the 2026 midterm elections, raising questions about MAHA’s political future.

Despite its name, MAHA has become a controversial force in American health politics. While the movement calls for healthier food, increased physical activity and greater corporate transparency, prominent figures within it have also challenged established scientific evidence, especially on vaccines.

Some commentators and critics have described the defeat of MAHA-aligned candidates like Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn as a “brutal election night wipeout.” Others have asked whether MAHA is “dying.”

Yet many Americans still support MAHA and the policies it champions. Its supporters also continue to hold powerful positions in the Trump administration – like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, and Kyle Diamantas, acting commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration – even as a new Congress prepares to take office in January 2027.

We are political scientists who study public opinion on healthcare policy. We see MAHA’s electoral losses as a political setback, not a death sentence. The movement’s influence extends beyond its candidates and the elections they contest.
MAHA’s electoral losses came amid a potentially generational swing toward Democrats across the country,

More than half the 24 gubernatorial and Congressional candidates endorsed by MAHA’s political action committee, MAHA Action, lost their election bids. These included Lahn, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton and House candidate Vic Mellor in Rhode Island. Others, like incumbent Representative Anna Paulina Luna, R-FL, won by less than 1% in a district that she won by nearly 10 percentage points in 2024.

Lahn’s defeat stands out as a major loss. Lahn, a farmer who railed against pesticides on the campaign trail and promised to ban COVID-19 vaccinations in Iowa, was endorsed by Kennedy. Lahn has been described by some as a model MAHA candidate and received over US$1 million in campaign contributions from MAHA Action.
Public support remains strong

But the movement’s poor showing at the ballot box does not mean that some of MAHA’s ideas are unpopular among Americans. A May 2026 poll conducted by the health policy organization KFF found that 41% of American adults supported MAHA, including many Democrats and independents.

Many Americans also share MAHA’s concerns about food safety. According to KFF, 75% of Americans believe the government does too little to regulate chemical additives in food, while 64% say the same about agricultural pesticides.

Yet the popularity of MAHA policies did little to help MAHA-backed candidates win in the first election cycle where MAHA-aligned candidates were on the ballot. Following the midterm elections, some MAHA activists moved to blame President Donald Trump for failing to fulfill promises on these issues.

One prime example: In a postelection episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, accused senior White House officials of allowing corporate interests to undermine MAHA’s goals. Dissatisfaction also spilled over to MAHA supporters in the general public, with one postelection poll finding that just over half of MAHA supporters feel the Trump administration made Americans’ health and well-being better throughout his second term in office.

Dissatisfaction with Trump, however, tells only part of the story. Another KFF poll conducted just before the election found that 42% of MAHA-supporting voters considered lowering healthcare costs their top health priority. By comparison, 21% prioritized restricting food additives, and 10% chose vaccine safety. Among voters more broadly, 55% believed Trump’s policies increased their healthcare costs, and 83% of those voters reported voting for Democrats. Most MAHA supporters, however, continued to vote for Republicans.

Supporting a movement, embracing its policy priorities and casting a ballot for its candidates do not necessarily go hand in hand. Americans can support MAHA’s goals without identifying with the movement or voting for its candidates. Likewise, MAHA supporters may vote Republican even when they are dissatisfied with Trump’s health policies. MAHA’s electoral losses, therefore, tell us little about how much support its ideas enjoy.
MAHA remains the status quo in Washington

Despite its electoral losses, MAHA still holds considerable influence in Washington. Kennedy still leads HHS, where he can continue reshaping how the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention steers vaccine recommendations in a direction that aligns with his vaccine-skeptical views. These efforts face growing scrutiny amid public confusion over Kennedy’s vaccine guidance and reports that he sought to remove measles-related deaths from CDC statistics.

Kennedy appears undeterred by MAHA’s electoral setbacks. Following the election, he praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, declaring, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.”

MAHA’s continued influence in the Trump administration, however, will face new obstacles now that Democrats control Congress. Facing greater opposition, the administration may increasingly rely on executive actions, including executive orders, new federal regulations and agency reports, to advance its health policies. However, Congress can also investigate HHS decisions and use its control over federal spending to limit what the agency can do.

MAHA’s political future remains uncertain. Some supporters may gradually move toward Democrats, particularly those concerned about corporate influence, pharmaceutical industry accountability and food safety. These concerns cross partisan lines, giving Democrats an opportunity to appeal to voters dissatisfied with Trump but still supportive of MAHA’s priorities.

MAHA could also become a movement independent of Trump and MAGA. It could bring together Americans who care about health and wellness, distrust major institutions and oppose corporate influence over food and medicine. Kennedy’s independent presidential campaign attracted as much as 15% support among voters in July 2024. This showed that an alternative to the two major parties could attract substantial support.

Whether MAHA remains tied to Trump’s increasingly divided coalition will shape its future beyond his presidency. The frustrations and health concerns that fueled its rise among Americans have not disappeared.

articles.title: Early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood – new study
articles.author: Justin Stebbing, Professor of Biomedical Sciences, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: The most common type of ovarian cancer tends to grow quickly. It’s called high-grade serous ovarian cancer and often starts in a fallopian tube, one of the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries towards the womb.

The first changes can be so small that they’re usually found only when a specialist examines the tube under a microscope after surgery. Now, a new study suggests that some of those changes may leave a trace in the blood.

The researchers looked for a molecule called Tu-stroma in stored blood samples. They found higher levels in people with early cancer that had begun growing into nearby tissue. Levels were also higher in people with a tiny patch of abnormal cells still confined to the lining of the fallopian tube. This patch, known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (Stic for short), can be an early step towards this type of ovarian cancer. The next step is to follow people over time to find out when the signal first appears.

Ovarian cancer can cause symptoms such as persistent bloating and pain in the tummy or low down between the hips. Some people feel full after eating very little or need to pee more often. These symptoms are common in other conditions too. If they persist or keep coming back, it’s worth getting them checked by a GP.

When investigating symptoms, doctors may use a blood test for CA125, a protein whose level can rise when ovarian cancer is present. Other conditions can raise it too, including endometriosis, in which tissue similar to the womb lining grows elsewhere in the body. Some people with early ovarian cancer still have a low CA125 level. The UK has no routine screening programme to check people without symptoms for ovarian cancer.
What the researchers found

Tu-stroma is a type of RNA, one of the molecules cells use to control how they work. Earlier research showed that ovarian cancer cells can release Tu-stroma in tiny packages called extracellular vesicles. Think of these as microscopic parcels carrying messages from one cell to another. The researchers measured how much Tu-stroma these parcels were carrying in the blood.

They analysed samples from 506 people, including 43 with Stic alone. In a separate group used to check how well the test worked, it picked up Stic in about 92% of those who had it. The test showed no signs of Stic in about 98% of people in the healthy comparison group. In these samples, Tu-stroma did a better job than CA125 of telling people with Stic apart from people who were healthy or had non-cancerous growths around the ovaries or fallopian tubes.

There’s an important catch. The researchers were working with samples from people whose diagnoses were already known. Only a small number had Stic, so the results are still uncertain. If the test were offered widely to people without symptoms, very few would be likely to have these patches of abnormal cells. Even a small proportion of false alarms could send many people for unnecessary tests or even surgery.
What it could mean for people at higher risk

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are genes that help repair damage to DNA, the genetic instructions in our cells. People who inherit a harmful change in either gene have a higher risk of ovarian cancer. They may be advised to consider surgery to remove their ovaries and fallopian tubes once they have finished having children or if they do not plan to have them. The operation lowers their risk, but it ends their ability to get pregnant without fertility treatment. If they haven’t yet reached menopause, the sudden drop in hormones after surgery brings it on straight away.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) advises that specialist teams can consider regular CA125 testing for some people at high inherited risk who delay or decline surgery. Tu-stroma might one day improve that monitoring. For now, even if the experimental test picks up no warning signs, that result gives someone no basis to postpone recommended surgery.

A large UK trial found that screening with CA125 picked up more ovarian and fallopian tube cancers at an early stage. Even after years of follow-up, there was no clear evidence that fewer people died from those cancers. With Tu-stroma, researchers still need to find out how often the abnormal cells in the tube lining start growing into nearby tissue. They also need to work out what to do if the blood test flags a problem but a scan shows nothing. The question a screening trial would ultimately have to answer is whether acting on that result saves lives.

articles.title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution
articles.author: Li Li (李黎), Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Penn State
paras: Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities that can fuel harmful algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “blue baby syndrome.”

But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of nitrogen that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.

In a new study, my colleague and I found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are associated with high river nitrate concentrations, even in places with little farming or urban development.

We found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is scarce, we found that nitrates – which can naturally leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or flushed away.

That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.

To see how widespread this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to estimate long-term average nitrate concentrations across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.
The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and agricultural regions where they are usually monitored.

High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Blue baby syndrome, or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate poisoning.
The U.S. drinking water standard of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.
We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers exceed the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.

That doesn’t mean 37,000 people are drinking water at those concentrations, since river water in many regions is treated before it is supplied for drinking. But it’s a concerning level they should be aware of, particularly those using well water.

Research has also raised concerns about possible effects of long-term exposure to nitrate at lower concentrations, including certain cancers and adverse birth outcomes, such as babies born preterm or with a low birth weight, although those risks are still being studied.
We estimate that about 480 million people worldwide live in areas where nearby rivers have elevated long-term average nitrate concentrations, above 2.5 milligrams per liter.

Many of the rivers our models identified as having elevated nitrate levels are small headwater streams. Many headwater streams cease to flow for some periods of time every year, and nitrates can accumulate to high concentrations under dry or low-flow conditions. These small streams make up most of the global river networks, have long been overlooked and feed larger rivers that supply drinking water to large populations and help shape the quality of water downstream.
Too much nitrate in rivers and lakes can also fuel algal growth and disrupt aquatic ecosystems.

A global map of nitrate concentrations in river water cannot show what comes out of someone’s tap. Their water may be mixed with other sources or treated before they drink it. Nitrate concentrations can also rise and fall over time, while our map shows long-term averages.
To understand a person’s actual exposure will require connecting river measurements with drinking water sources, treatment practices and tests of water delivered to households.

Many rivers with nitrate concentrations above 2.5 milligrams per liter flow through sparsely populated regions where access to treated drinking water may be limited. Even where treatment facilities exist, conventional methods remove little nitrate. Removing it requires specialized technologies that can be costly to operate.

Our study shows why more drylands and small headwater streams need to be monitored for nitrate. It also raises a question for a warming world: If a region becomes drier, how much will nitrate concentrations rise even if people do not add more nitrogen to the landscape?

Answering that will require measurements through wet and dry periods, paired with studies of how water moves through soils, groundwater and rivers. For now, the message is clear: Protecting water quality requires paying attention to the climate as well as to the human activities that put nitrogen into the environment.

articles.title: What is ‘food is medicine’? – 2 experts explain this decades-old approach to healthcare that is taking on new life
articles.author: Meagen Rosenthal, Associate Professor of Pharmacy Administration, University of Mississippi
paras: Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.

This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.

As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.

Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.

Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.

Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.

Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”

But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.

In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.

Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community

Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.

One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.

For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.

Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.

However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.

Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.

Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal receives funding from the State of Mississippi and the US Department of Agriculture.

articles.title: Rural women in Colorado and nationwide are at higher risk for cervical cancer – at-home test kits can help close the gap
articles.author: Christine Conageski, Professor of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: With vaccines and regular screening, cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers.
Yet women living in rural areas of the United States have a 25% higher rate of cervical cancer – and a 42% higher rate of death from the disease compared to urban women.
In Colorado, rural counties such as Prowers, Moffat and Montrose have almost three times the rate of cervical cancer than urban counties.

Nationwide, 13,000 women are diagnosed with the disease and more than 4,000 die from it each year. In Colorado, the most recent data available indicated that almost 150 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2023, and, on average, more than 40 women die annually.

While overall numbers of diagnoses and deaths nationwide have decreased over the past 20 years, rural women are more likely to be diagnosed at a later stage of disease, meaning chemotherapy and radiation treatments may be necessary to treat their disease.

My research and clinical expertise in gynecology and obstetrics specifically aim to tackle this troubling health disparity. I study lower genital tract precancers from human papillomavirus, or HPV. As part of a team of researchers across the U.S., I participated in a clinical trial that led to the first FDA-approved at-home HPV test.

The development of an at-home test is a game changer. It can bring screening to a broader spectrum of women, hopefully catching those who have precancerous changes early enough to prevent the progression to cancer.
But eliminating cervical cancer will require ensuring that women can access not only screening but also vaccines and any necessary follow-up diagnostic procedures and treatments.
A simple swab test at home

For rural women, access to healthcare clinics for routine screenings may be limited. A visit to a qualified professional for a cervical exam and Pap test can require half a day or longer in travel and wait times. In a recent study, women in rural counties were 20% less likely to be up to date on cervical cancer screening.

In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized the Teal Wand for at-home self-collection. Federal and medical organizations have since included self-collection as part of routine screening recommendations. My university received funding from Teal Health to support research. I was a site investigator, but I have no shares in the company or any patents, and I have never received any money directly from Teal.
Women can now also do a test during a visit to their primary care doctor even if that doctor does not perform pelvic exams. That means patients do not need to see a gynecologist to get screened.

Nearly all cervical cancers are caused by persistent viral infections from HPV. These infections most frequently occur through sexual contact. At-home screening tests check for infection, which means clinicians can identify women at risk of developing cervical cancer before the disease occurs.
During self-collection, women use a simple swab to collect a vaginal sample. That swab is mailed to the lab and then tested for HPV.
Studies have shown that when FDA-approved HPV tests are used, self-collected samples are as reliable as clinician-collected samples for detecting cervical precancer.

Studies show that self-collection tests for HPV can help decrease barriers to care for rural communities. A study across four Appalachian state regions – Ohio, West Virginia, Kentucky and Virginia – found that screening increases when women are mailed a self-collection kit. Appalachia, a largely rural geographic region that is underserved in terms of access to healthcare, has documented disparities in cervical cancer rates.

Underscreened patients across these four states were randomly chosen to either receive the usual care, a mailed reminder letter to go to a clinic or a mailed HPV self-collection kit. The study showed a threefold increase in screening rates: 5% with the reminder and 15% with the mailed kits.
Another study in Washington state showed similar results, with an increase in screening of overdue individuals by more than 15% in mailed kits versus education alone.

Statewide initiatives in Alabama, with the Operation Wipe Out project, and in Texas, with the Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan, use self-screening as part of a strategy to eliminate cervical cancer.
In Colorado, I am part of a team working to implement a similar plan that we hope to initiate in 2027.

Studies in Europe have shown that self-collection has increased access to care, improved screening rates and reduced screening costs. Long-term evidence demonstrates these programs are effective: Many countries began using them as early as 2017.

Making screening easier is only the first step toward preventing cervical cancer. Even in the Appalachian study, fewer than 15 out of 100 women who received mailed HPV self-collection kits completed screening.
In short, removing the need for a clinic visit does not address all the barriers to preventing this disease.
Screening combined with vaccines and mobile clinics

HPV vaccines are the single strongest tool for preventing cervical cancer. Vaccinations are recommended for adolescents ages 9-14 before they are exposed to HPV. If given under age 15, two shots six months apart are required. No booster is needed. Individuals who do not receive the vaccine before turning 15 can get a “catch-up” vaccine as a three-shot series up to age 45.

For women who test positive for high-risk HPV, additional testing may be necessary to identify precancerous changes in the cervix. In rural communities, accessing these services can be even more challenging than obtaining screening.

Mobile clinics can bring services closer to patients. Training more clinicians to provide colposcopy services could improve access to diagnostic care. Colposcopy is an exam in which a healthcare provider uses a lighted magnifying instrument to look closely at the cervix for abnormal or precancerous changes. A small tissue sample may be taken for diagnostic testing.

Patient navigators and community health workers can also assist women in overcoming barriers to care. A patient navigator is a trained professional who helps overcome roadblocks by providing education, coordinating services, connecting patients with resources and supporting them through the healthcare system to ensure timely access to care.
Rural women in Colorado and elsewhere urgently need a concerted effort from statewide programs and health centers to decrease the incidence and deaths from this disease.
No one should die from cervical cancer.
Christine Conageski received research funding from Teal Health, Inc. She is affiliated with the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP).

articles.title: El Niño threatens health, too – early warnings done right can save lives
articles.author: Kimberley Miner, Research Professor in Earth Sciences, University of Maine
paras: As communities around the world shore up their infrastructure in anticipation of one of the most powerful El Niños on record in late 2026 and early 2027, they need to think about rising health risks, too – and include them in early weather warnings.

El Niño is part of a natural climate phenomenon that shifts global weather patterns for months at a time. During El Niño years, global temperatures tend to rise, triggering heat waves; normally dry regions can be hit with flooding rainfall; and normally wet regions often face droughts. All carry serious health risks.

In southern Africa, for example, forecasters are warning of a rising risk of severe drought that could affect the 2026-27 growing season in key farming regions. At the same time, wetter-than-normal conditions in the Horn of Africa raise the risk of flooding and mosquito-borne disease outbreaks there.

Dry conditions in Southeast Asia are already fueling wildfires and sending water supplies falling. October downpours in Chile triggered mudslides that left a mess for people to clean up in homes and yards.
In the United States, the South tends to be wetter than normal during El Niño years; drought is more likely in the Northern Plains; and storms can be fierce, particularly along the Pacific Coast.
As researchers in psychology, global health and Earth system science, we study how environmental disruptions affect people’s health and their ability to respond.
To protect the population, communities need plans that keep care accessible and weather warnings that provide advice people can act on before, during and after a disaster.
When extreme weather becomes a health emergency
The health consequences of extreme weather events often extend beyond the immediate hazard.
For example, research has linked exposure to flooding, wildfire and ecosystem changes with elevated risks of illnesses, psychological distress and chronic stress.

Floodwater can lead to infections, such as hepatitis, cryptosporidium and fungal diseases, as well as longer-term health damage through exposure to harmful environmental microbes, chemicals and an increase in disease-carrying vectors such as mosquitoes.
Drought can lead to poor air quality and, in some places, malnutrition.
Disasters can also keep people from getting essential healthcare, disrupt their livelihoods and displace them from their homes and social networks.

The threat of a changing, potentially unsafe environment can also increase anticipatory, long-term distress. The World Health Organization identifies anxiety and post-traumatic stress as mental health consequences of extreme weather-related hazards. We believe mental health counseling services also belong in communities’ preparedness and recovery plans, not as an optional add-on after addressing physical needs.
Vulnerable populations face even higher risks

For people with existing illnesses or in areas far from medical care, extreme weather brings additional risks. These individuals and healthcare systems benefit from early warnings about El Niño’s disaster risks that help them prepare well in advance.

At least 2.5 million Americans rely on in-home electricity-powered medical equipment, such as oxygen concentrators and ventilators, including nearly 78,000 who receive dialysis at home to help their kidneys function. When the power goes out or water is disrupted, they risk losing use of what may be life-sustaining equipment.

Distance compounds these risks. Many communities around the world don’t have local clinics. Rural Americans live an average of 10.5 miles (17 kilometers) from the nearest hospital, and for 1 in 4 rural residents, the trip takes more than 30 minutes on average – before a single road floods. During Hurricane Harvey in 2017, flooding limited access to Houston’s second-busiest hospital for five days. The most extensive disruptions were in lower-income and minority neighborhoods.

With advanced warnings, community organizations and healthcare providers preparing for El Niño can contact people with health vulnerabilities early to arrange backup power supplies and help them prepare so they know what to do when disasters do strike.
How to turn forecasts into protection
A good weather warning doesn’t just name the threat. It also provides information that residents can act on to stay safe through the disaster and the recovery afterward.

Communities do not need to wait until a disaster is building to begin preparing. Existing community emergency plans, patient outreach programs and social networks provide a starting point for steps that help.
First, communities can identify where disruptions could become public health emergencies.

State departments of health and other social services can combine regional weather outlooks with local information about areas facing the highest risks, including the health impacts of water exposure on homes, guidance for avoiding polluted floodwaters and evacuation routes.
Community organizations can help identify individuals and neighborhoods that may face language barriers and ensure they receive lifesaving alerts and information they can understand.
Second, it’s important to protect continuity of clinical care for patients during disasters.

Health systems and public health departments can coordinate with health providers in hospitals, pharmacies and home health services to identify people who depend on regular medical appointments or transportation and ensure they can still receive care.
In practice, this may be providing flexible scheduling options, organizing alternative means of transportation or identifying alternative care locations that may be more accessible.
Third, weather warnings can be most useful when they provide information people can act on, such as where to find food, transportation or mental health support.

Many local and state emergency services already work to educate the public about storm risks ahead. They can do more by also telling residents where they can find safe water and food, how to limit exposure to chemicals or disease vectors, how to store medicine safely, and whom to contact for transportation, shelter or mental health support.
Information that is specific enough to use and relevant to the community can save lives.
Preparation is preventive care

Because signs of the coming weather shift can be detected months in advance, El Niño forecasts offer something that immediate storm forecasts can’t: extra time to identify these health risks, secure medical care for the months ahead and prepare so warnings are useful to residents.
When warnings pair information about the risk with practical actions and local resources, they can empower people rather than leaving them feeling helpless in the face of a disaster.

articles.title: Collagen powders, creams and bone broth: what the science says about their benefits
articles.author: Joan Chang, Senior Lecturer, Research, Division of Molecular and Cellular Function, University of Manchester
paras: Collagen is turning up in coffee, crisps and beauty creams, promising firmer skin and stronger joints. As someone who studies collagen, I find some of the claims rather optimistic.

I even gave collagen supplements to guests at my wedding, accompanied by a disclaimer that this was no endorsement of their effectiveness. The science is considerably more interesting than the marketing.

Collagen is a family of at least 28 proteins that help give the body its shape and strength. All share a distinctive structure: three chains twisted together, rather like strands of a rope. Some of these molecules assemble into larger fibres around cells that support skin, tendons and bones. Other types form thin supporting networks separating different body compartments.

Collagen is part of the extracellular matrix, the mesh of proteins and other materials surrounding our cells. Cells make collagen using amino acids, the building blocks of all proteins, and release it outside themselves to build and maintain tissues.

As we age, keeping this structure in good repair becomes harder. The amount of collagen produced can change, but existing collagen also becomes altered. Some fibres last extraordinarily long: carbon-dating research suggests the central part of the human Achilles tendon contains collagen laid down during the first 17 years of life, with very little replacement in adulthood.

Over time, chemical bonds can form between collagen molecules making the tissue less flexible. So having more collagen does not necessarily mean having healthier collagen. How it is assembled, maintained and replaced also matters.
Does eating collagen replenish it?
Many supplements contain hydrolysed collagen: collagen that has already been broken into smaller pieces. Gelatine, familiar from gummy sweets, is another processed form of collagen.

After you swallow collagen, digestion breaks it down further into amino acids and short chains called peptides. Some of these reach the bloodstream. But they do not arrive in your cheeks or knees as ready-made collagen fibres. Cells may reuse those building blocks to make proteins, or for other purposes.
So is collagen powder any better than getting enough protein from ordinary food? It’s an important question, and one we cannot yet answer confidently.

Human trials of oral collagen supplements have produced mixed results. A 2025 analysis of 23 trials found improvements in skin hydration and elasticity overall, but no statistically significant benefits when higher-quality studies were examined separately. A newer review of 35 trials reported improvements in hydration and some measures of elasticity, but found no reliable evidence of reduced wrinkles or increased skin density. These findings do not establish whether taking collagen offers any advantage over eating an adequate, balanced diet.

Bone broth is another source of collagen-derived protein. I enjoy it as part of the diet I grew up eating, but swallowing broth does not specifically replace collagen in your joints, at least not evidenced by science. Its nutritional value depends on the ingredients and preparation.
Can creams and treatments do more?

Collagen creams face another obstacle: the skin is a protective barrier. Intact collagen molecules are generally too large to pass through it. A cream may make your skin feel smoother by helping it retain water without delivering new collagen to deeper layers.

There is better evidence for protecting the collagen you already have. Ultraviolet radiation from sunlight can increase collagen breakdown, making sunscreen important. Studies also suggest that retinoids, ingredients related to vitamin A, can improve fine wrinkles and stimulate collagen production, although they can irritate skin.

I’m also cautious about skincare containing PDRN, fragments of DNA often promoted as being derived from salmon sperm. A review of clinical trials suggests PDRN may help damaged skin heal, including by speeding up wound repair.

But these findings don’t necessarily apply to ordinary face creams. Wounded skin has a damaged protective barrier, whereas healthy skin makes it much harder for large molecules such as PDRN to penetrate. Whether enough PDRN can reach the deeper layers of intact skin to produce meaningful benefits remains uncertain.

Microneedling works differently. Tiny needles create controlled injuries, setting off repair processes that can stimulate collagen formation. Clinical studies suggest benefits for some acne scars, but the procedure can cause infection, pigmentation changes or further scarring, especially when hygiene and technique are poor.

Home microneedling rollers – handheld devices covered in tiny needles that are rolled across the skin – also carry risks. Pressing too hard or repeatedly treating the same area can damage the skin, potentially causing lasting discolouration or scarring. Poorly cleaned devices can introduce bacteria, while rolling over infected areas can spread viruses such as herpes across the skin.
The American Academy of Dermatology also warns that home devices generally produce less noticeable results than professional treatments, so the potential benefits may be limited.
The surprising connection with sleep

My research has found that collagen maintenance follows a daily rhythm in mouse tendons. The animals’ cells produced and assembled collagen at different times, and disrupting their internal body clocks affected the fibres they formed.

Later work showed that cells can take up existing collagen and recycle it into new fibres. This recycling process was altered in cells associated with fibrosis, a condition in which excessive scar-like tissue builds up in an organ.

In the lungs, this can make breathing difficult. These are early findings about how tissues maintain collagen, not proof that a particular bedtime will improve human skin, although it is clear that sleep disruption wreaks havoc on our body in general.
Nor does eating collagen cause fibrosis. The point is that the body must regulate how much collagen it makes and how it organises and removes it.

For now, I would prioritise a balanced diet, physical activity, consistent sleep and sun protection over expensive promises to “boost collagen”. Looking after the systems that maintain our tissues is more sensible than assuming a scoop of powder will rebuild them.

articles.title: You likely have genes that affect how well your medications work – testing for them could improve treatment
articles.author: Philip Empey, Associate Professor, University of Pittsburgh School of Pharmacy, University of Pittsburgh
paras: All people carry differences in their DNA that could affect how they respond to medication, according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.

Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA.

The field of pharmacogenomics studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your liver breaks down a drug and how long it stays in your bloodstream.

But using genetic testing to guide prescriptions is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been done on people of European ancestry, researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.
Genetic variants and drugs

To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers and I analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program. All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research.

We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.

We found that every participant carried at least one relevant genetic variant, and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.

Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is affected by a genetic variant they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.

These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs.
Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.
Improving precision medicine

Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance precision medicine.

However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also affect how the body processes drugs.
Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.
Philip Empey receives funding from the NIH, Veterans Administration, Shear Family Foundation and Myers Family Foundation.

articles.title: Hot or cold? Our research explores what works best after exercise
articles.author: Freya Bayne, Lecturer, Sport and Exercise Science, University of East London
paras: Ice baths have become one of the most popular recovery strategies in sport. They are used by elite athletes and recreational gym-goers to reduce soreness and recuperate more quickly after exercising.

It has often been claimed that ice baths help to reduce pain and repair the muscle damage that intense exercise can cause. Yet when we look at the evidence, it isn’t clear that ice baths really are the best way to recover post exercise.
In a recent study, my colleagues and I compared ice baths against heat-based recovery methods. What we found suggests recovery is far more complex than simply cooling things down.

Strenuous or unfamiliar exercise can cause damage to our muscle fibres. This is particularly the case after doing “eccentric exercises”, where muscles lengthen while generating force. Activities such as downhill running, descending the stairs or lowering a weight under control (while doing a barbell squat for instance) are all examples of eccentric exercise.

This exercise-induced muscle damage can leave your muscles feeling sore and weak. To repair the damage, the body triggers what’s known as an “inflammatory repair response”, where immune cells move into the muscle tissue to clear away damaged cellular material and stimulate regeneration.

Other molecules are also released to help coordinate repair. However, these molecules can also increase the sensitivity of pain receptors, which may further contribute to the muscle soreness that people experience up to 72 hours after an intense workout.
These responses are an important part of how the body repairs itself and becomes stronger.

We wanted to better understand what effect different recovery methods had on this repair process after a strenuous workout. So we recruited 40 healthy, physically active adults (31 men and nine women) and asked them to complete a specific exercise.

This involved repeatedly targeting the quadriceps – the large muscles at the front of the thigh – using a specialised machine that allowed us to carefully control the movement and measure muscle strength. This particular movement is known to cause temporary muscle damage and soreness – making it useful for studying how different recovery methods influence the body’s repair process.

Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four recovery methods: cold-water immersion (in water that was 10°C), hot-water immersion (in water that was 42°C), hot air exposure (60°C, similar to a sauna) and “passive recovery” which involved sitting and doing nothing for 30 minutes. Each method was carried out immediately after the workout.

Over the following 72 hours, we monitored recovery by looking at several measures – including muscle strength, pain and soreness, alongside various biological markers linked to muscle damage, inflammation and cellular stress.
All participants showed the expected signs of exercise-induced muscle damage. Strength declined immediately after exercise and soreness increased.
But when we looked at the effects of the recovery techniques, we were surprised to find that none of them restored muscle strength significantly faster than the others.
If strength had been the only outcome measured, we might have concluded the recovery methods made little difference. But the physiological data told a different story.

Participants who completed hot-water immersion were shown to have higher levels of a substance called “heat shock protein 72” (HSP72) which acts as a cellular maintenance and protection system, supporting repair processes and protecting cells during periods of physiological stress. It’s widely believed that HSP72 plays an important role in recovery and adaptation following exercise.
The heat-based recovery methods were also associated with more favourable changes in biological markers linked to muscle damage and inflammation.
So our findings suggest that exposure to heat may be better at stimulating the biological processes involved in recovery.

Cold-water immersion was not shown to improve any of the recovery markers measured in the study. It also showed the slowest recovery, with strength returning to around 82% of pre-exercise levels after 72 hours, compared with 88-89% in the other groups.

But cold-water immersion appeared more effective at reducing perceptions of muscle soreness. This highlights how feeling recovered and actually being physiologically recovered are not always the same thing.

These findings should be interpreted with some caution, however. The study involved 40 healthy, physically active adults – with just ten participants in each intervention group. While the study was adjusted to detect moderate effects, the sample size wasn’t large enough to explore potential differences between men and women.
One of the most important lessons from our study is that recovery cannot be measured using a single outcome.
A person may feel less sore but may still have reduced muscle function. Also, important repair processes may be occurring inside the body without producing immediate improvements in performance.
This distinction may help explain why recovery research has produced mixed findings over the years. Different interventions may influence different aspects of recovery.

If your priority is reducing how sore you feel after a workout, cold-water immersion may be the most beneficial. But if your goal is to influence the biological processes that help your muscles to repair and adapt, heat-based recovery may be a better choice.
Our findings don’t suggest that ice baths are completely ineffective. Ice baths were still found to help people feel better.
What our study shows is that recovery is about far more than how you feel the next day. Sometimes the most important changes are happening beneath the surface.

articles.title: Blood sugar spikes: what actually works to manage them
articles.author: Gulshanara (Rumy) Begum, Senior Lecturer in Nutrition & Exercise Science, University of Westminster
paras: Blood sugar, also called blood glucose, rises after eating. Seeing that rise on a wearable monitor can make an ordinary meal look worrying. But a higher reading after lunch does not, by itself, mean that something has gone wrong.

The body uses glucose for energy. After a meal containing carbohydrate, glucose enters the bloodstream. In response, the pancreas, an organ behind the stomach, releases insulin. This hormone helps the body use glucose and store some for later.

For people with diabetes, managing blood glucose is essential. For people without diabetes, however, the benefits of tracking every rise and trying to flatten it are much less certain. A recent review found important gaps between claims about harmful “glucose spikes” and the available research.
So what can everyday habits do, and how much should we expect from them?

The type and amount of carbohydrate you eat affect how much your blood glucose rises after eating. Choosing fibre-rich foods, such as beans and wholegrains, is a good place to start. A review of clinical trials found that increasing fibre improved measures of blood glucose control in people with diabetes or prediabetes; where glucose levels are above the usual range but below the threshold for diabetes.

Another way of comparing foods that contain carbohydrates is the glycaemic index, or GI. It compares how much they raise blood glucose when portions containing the same amount of carbohydrate are eaten.

But GI tells only part of the story. It does not account for the portion you actually eat or the other foods on your plate. A food’s GI therefore cannot tell you exactly how your body will respond to a whole meal.

Other ingredients in a meal can change how high blood glucose rises and when it peaks. Adding fat, for example, may delay the rise without necessarily reducing the overall glucose response. A lower early peak does not, on its own, mean that a meal is healthier.

It may also matter which foods you eat first. A 2026 review of six small studies, involving 107 healthy adults, found that eating vegetables or protein-rich foods before carbohydrate-rich foods often reduced the rise in blood glucose shortly after eating.
However, these short studies, mainly involving young adults, do not show whether eating foods in a particular order prevents diabetes or improves long term health.
Movement can help your body use glucose
When muscles contract, they can take up glucose from the blood through processes that do not depend entirely on insulin.

Regular exercise has much more evidence behind it than individual post-meal movement strategies. A review of 100 randomised trials in adults with type 2 diabetes found that aerobic exercise, such as cycling, and resistance exercise, such as lifting weights, helped lower HbA1c. This is a measure of average blood glucose levels over the previous two to three months. Lower HbA1c levels generally indicate better long-term blood glucose control, which can help reduce the risk of diabetes-related complications.

Movement after eating may also help. A review of studies involving people with type 2 diabetes found that exercise after meals could reduce the subsequent glucose rise. The studies differed considerably, so they could not establish one ideal exercise routine or starting time.

Even a short walk may make a difference. In a small trial involving 12 healthy young adults, participants had a lower glucose response over two hours when they walked at a comfortable pace for ten minutes immediately after drinking a glucose solution than when they remained seated.

That is encouraging, but a glucose drink differs from dinner. The study cannot tell us exactly what a ten-minute walk will do after an ordinary meal for people of different ages and health backgrounds.

Researchers have also investigated seated “soleus push-ups”: repeated heel raises that work a muscle deep in the calf. In a 2025 pilot study, ten people with prediabetes had a lower glucose response while repeating the movement throughout a two-hour test involving a glucose drink test. This does not show that a few heel raises after lunch would have the same effect or improve glucose control over time.
Sleep matters too. Glucose regulation also depends on how effectively the body responds to insulin, known as insulin sensitivity.

A review combining results from randomised studies found that restricting sleep reduced insulin sensitivity in healthy adults. This supports paying attention to sleep alongside food and activity, although it does not show that an extra hour in bed will produce a particular glucose reading.

Wearable continuous glucose monitors use a small sensor beneath the skin to measure glucose in the fluid between cells and estimate glucose levels. They can be valuable in diabetes care, but current diagnostic guidance says there is insufficient evidence to use them to diagnose diabetes or prediabetes.

Diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests, usually with a second abnormal result to confirm the diagnosis unless it is already clear. A standard glucose-tolerance test uses a measured glucose drink, so its diagnostic thresholds cannot simply be applied to a reading after an ordinary meal.
People with diabetes need advice tailored to their medication and circumstances. Some treatments, including insulin, can cause dangerously low blood glucose, so lower readings are not always better.

For most people without diabetes, there is no established need to flatten every rise after eating. Focus instead on sustainable habits, such as including more fibre-rich foods, moving regularly and getting adequate sleep, rather than judging each meal by a glucose graph. If you repeatedly see unexpected readings or have symptoms that concern you, seek medical advice.

articles.title: GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect
articles.author: Ziyad Al-Aly, Clinical Epidemiologist, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a potential link to a rare eye condition that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a stroke of the eye.
I am a clinician and epidemiologist who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION.

Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an expanding list of clinical conditions.

The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so.
Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect.

NAION is an injury to the optic nerve, which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness.

These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower.
How did the FDA identify the connection?

As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since 2021, when they were approved for obesity – cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported an increased risk of the eye condition among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug.

To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the FDA first compiled data from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison.

Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs.

In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of sentinel programs that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024.

Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs.
Is there other evidence of the risk?

Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION.

For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly 600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients.

That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk.

What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this.

The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect.

The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence – the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently – points in the same direction.

But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of.
Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug – and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it.

Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems. For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have risk factors for it, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important.

articles.title: RFK Jr. loosens access to unapproved peptides: A health law scholar explains what consumers need to know
articles.author: Ana Santos Rutschman, Professor of Law, Villanova University
paras: Unregulated peptides for weight loss, muscle building, longevity and more are a roaring wellness fad – even though these substances have not been proved safe and effective and have not been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Until now, consumers were getting wellness peptides online through the so-called gray market, where companies rely on legal loopholes to sell them. Due to a push from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a vocal proponent of using peptides, an HHS policy on Oct. 29, 2026, will expand access to six peptides by allowing specialized pharmacies to make and sell them.
I am a health law professor who researches and teaches FDA law and policy. Consumers of peptides will soon have more options, but they should also be aware of the risks.
Drugs versus wellness products

Peptides are short chains of amino acids, which are building blocks for proteins. More than 7,000 peptides occur naturally in the human body. Some peptides – both natural and synthetic – have been developed as medicines, such as insulin and GLP-1 drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy.

Peptides that are commercialized as pharmaceutical drugs go through clinical trials and are approved by the FDA. But the slew of “wellness” peptides promoted by influencers and sold online or at wellness stores are not evaluated by any regulator.

American consumers have been able to buy wellness peptides online for over a decade. Until 2023 some of these peptides were sold at some specialized pharmacies as well. But that year the FDA restricted access to several wellness peptides due to unnamed “significant safety concerns,” forbidding specialized pharmacies from making and selling them. This did not prevent consumers from buying peptides online and at stores, however.

Since the early 2020s, the mainstreaming of wellness through the MAHA movement has driven up consumer interest in peptides. Access to nonpharmaceutical, unapproved products such as wellness peptides have long been a cornerstone of Kennedy’s personal philosophy and of the MAHA agenda.

Earlier this year, Kennedy pushed the FDA to review several peptides that the agency had restricted in 2023. Kennedy appointed eight new members to the committee that advises the FDA on these matters, all of whom had ties to businesses selling or promoting peptides. In July 2026 the committee voted 8-6 to expand access to six peptides: BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and TB-500.

The vote came after FDA scientists repeatedly told the committee that there was not enough information about the safety and efficacy of the peptides to justify letting compounding pharmacies sell them.

Some of these peptides are very popular, particularly on social media. For example, wellness influencers refer to the combination of BPC-157 and TB-500 as the “Wolverine stack,” after the Marvel comics superhero, often recommending it for building muscle mass and speeding up postworkout recovery. Kennedy has promoted these peptides in podcasts and as part of his Take Back Your Health tour.
The new policy allows small compounding pharmacies to sell these six peptides.

Compounding pharmacies are licensed to produce and sell a very small set of drugs that are not reviewed and approved by the FDA. Compounded drugs require a prescription and are meant for patients for whom there is no appropriate drug that is commercially available. For example, patients might need a drug in a strength or form that’s not specifically FDA-approved.

Normally the FDA does not encourage the sale of unstudied products. In this case, the agency is using a policy tool known as enforcement discretion to let these pharmacies know that there will be no legal consequences if they sell the six listed wellness peptides. This policy is often described as having an agency look the other way.
What is enforcement discretion?

When an agency employs enforcement discretion, it means that the law gives it authority to regulate an area but it chooses not to use that authority. This typically happens when the regulator thinks that a product poses very low risk to the public.
For example, during a recent shortage of some weight-loss drugs, the FDA used enforcement discretion to allow some compounding pharmacies to produce the drug to help ease the shortage.

However, if the FDA chooses not to enforce the law and the product poses risks to consumers, the consequences can be severe. The most notable case involved certain types of diagnostic tests, including tests for Lyme disease and breast and ovarian cancer. Several tests were on the market for a long time. For example, a company called Genomic Health started selling a breast cancer screening test in 2008. In 2011 scientists began questioning the accuracy of the test. In 2014 it was confirmed the test had provided false negatives to cancer patients.

The type of blood test that Elizabeth Holmes and her collaborators at Theranos claimed to have developed also belonged to the category of tests over which the FDA was exercising enforcement discretion. That was one of the reasons no one was monitoring Theranos properly, and that helped Holmes and her company hide their fraud for a long time.
What consumers should know

Kennedy and other proponents of peptides have said that it would be better for consumers to be able to buy them at compounding pharmacies, rather than online or at wellness stores, because these pharmacies are licensed to produce some medications that have not been approved by the FDA.

The new policy’s wording echos this sentiment, which implies that oversight by a pharmacist would somehow make these substances safer. However, compounding pharmacies have no obligation to test any ingredients they obtain from outside suppliers.

There is very little oversight of what is actually sold at these pharmacies. Federal law requires the FDA to evaluate drugs before they can be sold and to monitor their production. These requirements do not apply to compounded drugs.
The FDA’s own website notes that the lack of FDA regulation opens the door to “poor compounding practices” and that some compounded products can be unsafe or ineffective.
Under the new policy, there will be more places selling these wellness peptides, but there will still be no regulator checking their safety and efficacy.

More broadly, the FDA’s choice not to regulate peptides can have long-term effects for commercial research. FDA law incentivizes companies to do research on their products. But its new policy on peptides signals that the agency is not interested in having these products studied and evaluated. In my view, that may discourage studies exploring their use, including research that could uncover novel applications for them.
