articles.title: Dark nutrition: what happens when people stop trusting food and nutrition science?
articles.author: Jordan Beaumont, Senior Lecturer in Food and Nutrition, Sheffield Hallam University
paras: “I’m Pi and this is Leo, and today we’re going to eat some raw roadkill.” So begins a YouTube video featuring two raw food enthusiasts eating the heart of a run-over raccoon.
Another of the duo’s YouTube videos is titled The Elite Know Raw Food is Safe & Healthy and Vilify it to Keep You a Weak Slave. That title neatly sums up the ethos of “dark nutrition”.

A New York Times Magazine article clarifies that dark nutrition is not a specific diet, but a style of thinking about food and health. “Its adherents [have] concluded that the usual sources of authority – doctors, public health officials, food executives, pharmaceutical corporations – [can] not be trusted,” the article explains.

People who follow this style of eating tend to reject mainstream dietary advice in favour of unconventional eating practices. This can include avoiding seed oils, drinking unpasteurised milk, consuming lots of sugar, avoiding vegetables, taking unusually high doses of supplements and, yes, even eating raw roadkill.

These food choices often stem from concerns about pesticides, toxins and pollutants in food. Or they can emerge when someone has an ailment their doctor can’t resolve. They take matters into their own hands and change the one thing they have complete control over: their diet.

Most people are satisfied with official nutritional guidance, but others seek more specific answers. As a result, those following dark nutrition self-experiment in an attempt to boost their health or treat a condition, regardless of whether there is scientific evidence to support their choices.

Some people get their nutrition information from the news, social media, and family and friends. But what is often covered in the headlines or on social media isn’t necessarily what is shown in the scientific studies.

The misleading information could be because journalists and influencers are not trained to understand the complex content of research papers, or because researchers are just really bad at explaining their findings. Even healthcare professionals and the government get it wrong occasionally. As a result, nutrition messages can become confused and confusing.

A great example is the humble egg. In 1957, the British Egg Marketing Board launched the campaign: “Go to work on an egg”. Then, in 1968, the American Heart Association recommended that people at high risk of heart disease eat no more than three eggs a week.

The recommendation was based partly on animal experiments linking blood cholesterol to coronary heart disease. However, the relationship between eating eggs and developing heart disease turned out to be considerably more complicated than early nutritional advice suggested.
By the 1990s, eggs were back in the good books. They are now widely considered a healthy and affordable source of protein, vitamins and minerals.
Margarine, red wine, coffee, coconut oil, red meat, potatoes and chocolate have had their own roller-coaster rides – one minute healthy, the next minute not.

This constant back-and-forth and changing messages can mean it is hard to know what constitutes a healthy diet. Unfortunately, nutrition science is messy, and it is a relatively young scientific discipline. Much of what we know has only been identified in the last century.
That means there are lots of questions that remain unanswered, and as we (nutritionists) search for the answers, we are likely to get things wrong. That is science.

Science is a process of questioning the world around us and searching for answers through research. The problem we have in nutrition research is that it is very hard to control someone’s diet and all the factors in their life that can affect health to provide definitive answers to the questions.

We mainly rely on people self-reporting the foods they eat and what illnesses or diseases they develop. This can tell us whether there is a link between diet and health, but not if diet prevents or causes illness and disease. So we have evidence that is seen as broad, conflicting and confusing.

Sadly, we now live in a post-truth era where scientific evidence is less important and influential than someone’s beliefs or opinions. The influencer culture – where people can share their own thoughts as fact, regardless of whether there is any foundation or evidence – has a big role to play in fuelling dark nutrition.

What is clear here is that the wider dangers of following dark nutrition are largely ignored. The potential for food poisoning, infection and disease by eating raw meat and organs, the risk of vitamin and mineral deficiencies by avoiding fruit and vegetables, and the chance of toxic levels of some vitamins and minerals with excessive supplement use.

It can be confusing to know what to eat. Government guidelines on food and nutrition remain the backbone of a healthy diet, and these will develop as new evidence emerges. Questioning conventional advice is reasonable, but alternative diets also need to be judged by the quality of the evidence.

Jordan Beaumont receives funding from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and Sheffield Children's Hospital Charity Trust. He is affiliated with the Association for the Study of Obesity and the Faculty of Public Health.

articles.title: Sewers could hold the key to detecting deadly fungal infections
articles.author: Pooja Padmakumar, PhD Candidate in Environmental Science, Bangor University
paras: Every year, fungal infections kill around 2.5 million people worldwide, more than tuberculosis and malaria combined. Yet most people may have never heard of the fungi responsible, and few health systems track them in any organised way.
In a recent review, my colleagues and I argue that one of the best places to start looking for these fungal pathogens is the sewer.

Fungi are all around us and most are harmless. A small number cause serious disease, mainly in people whose immune systems are weakened, for example by cancer treatment, an organ transplant or a stay in intensive care. The World Health Organization has published a list of priority fungal pathogens that it says urgently need better surveillance.

A warming climate, more people living with weakened immunity and a very small number of antifungal drugs are creating good conditions for dangerous fungi, so this threat is growing. Some are adapting to human body temperature, to hospital environments and to the medicines used against them.

One example is Candida auris. It was first identified in a patient’s ear in Japan in 2009. This yeast has since spread worldwide, it resists several drugs and it causes hospital outbreaks that are hard to control.

Despite this, fungi get little attention. Unlike flu or norovirus, fungal infections rarely look like an outbreak. They tend to be seen as a complication of someone’s existing illness rather than a public health threat in their own right. In the UK, labs have only been required to report C. auris since 2025.

In our review, we looked at why hospital-based monitoring misses fungi, and at what the early evidence says about testing wastewater instead. We found three main problems. The first is the one above: fungi are treated as a secondary concern.

The second is biology. Many people carry fungi such as Candida on their skin or in their gut for months or even years without feeling ill, and the whole time they are shedding the fungus. Hospital testing only picks up the minority who become seriously ill, so the true spread is underestimated.

The third problem is technical limitations. Fungal tests are limited, and there is little commercial incentive to improve them. Labs often don’t identify common yeasts down to the species level, so a drug-resistant species can go unnoticed.
Everyone uses the toilet, whether they are ill or not, and whether or not they ever see a doctor. That makes wastewater a snapshot of a whole community.
During COVID, virus levels in sewage rose four to 14 days before confirmed cases did. For fungi, the evidence is still thin, and almost all of it concerns C. auris.

In southern Nevada in the US, researchers found it in 79% of wastewater samples over ten weeks, more often in areas served by healthcare facilities. In Florida, 47% of hospital wastewater samples tested positive, compared with 16% at treatment plants further downstream. In a UK hospital, the fungus was found in the wastewater coming from one particular ward during an outbreak.

These studies show that the fungus can be detected in wastewater. They do not yet show that sewage data can predict outbreaks. Nobody yet knows how much of the fungus each person sheds, so a sewage reading can’t be turned into a number of patients.

Genetic tests detect fungal DNA but can’t tell whether the fungus is alive or drug-resistant. Because many Candida species live harmlessly in people, simply finding one tells us little. Combining genetic tests with growing samples in the lab will be needed. And some fungi, such as Aspergillus, are inhaled and won’t pass through the gut, so sewage may not reflect those infections at all. Recent research picked up several disease-causing yeasts from wastewater sources, suggesting the approach could work beyond C. auris.

Wastewater treatment doesn’t remove every pathogen, while storm overflow pipes can release untreated sewage directly into rivers and the sea. C. auris has been found on remote beaches in the Andaman Islands, India, which suggests it lived in the environment long before it reached hospitals. In Hong Kong’s mangroves, all the multidrug-resistant yeasts researchers found came from sites near wastewater treatment works.
Low levels of antifungal drugs reaching rivers and soil may favour resistant strains. This link is possible but not yet proven.

Wastewater monitoring would not replace hospital testing of patients. Its value would be in telling health services where to look, especially in places where testing people at scale isn’t possible. Researchers now need to standardise methods, measure how much fungus people shed, and work out what sewage levels should trigger action. The goal should be to link wastewater data with hospital, animal and farm monitoring.
The tools already exist, as COVID showed. What has been missing is the will to prioritise fungi before the next resistant one outpaces us.
Pooja Padmakumar receives funding from Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Digital Health Hub for AMR, project reference EP/X031276/1.

articles.title: The stroke risk younger adults may be overlooking – and the symptoms that should never be dismissed
articles.author: David Olawade, Lecturer, Department of Allied and Public Health, School of Health, Sport and Bioscience, University of East London
paras: Stroke is often seen as a condition that only affects older people. Yet the incidence of stroke in older people has actually fallen in recent decades. At the same time, rates of stroke in under-55s has been on the rise.

In England, stroke incidence among 35- to 54-year-olds rose by about 2% a year between 2001 and 2010, even as overall rates dropped. In Oxfordshire alone, stroke rates in under-55s were about 90% higher in 2010–2018 than in 1981–1986 – while rates in older people fell.
The US tells a similar story, with stroke rates in 20- to 54-year-olds rising from 34 to 62 cases per 100,000 people a year between 1993-1994 and 2020.

Globally, nearly 2.8 million people under 55 had a stroke in 2021, almost 90% of them in low- and middle-income countries. Between 2020 and 2030, it’s projected that rates of ischaemic stroke (the most common type, which is caused by a blood clot) among 20- to 39-year-olds will rise by about 12%.
What is fuelling the rise?
The rising rates of stroke in young people largely appears to be driven by things we can change.

A large international study identified ten modifiable risk factors which accounted for around 92% of strokes that occurred in people under 55. These factors included high blood pressure, physical inactivity, high cholesterol, poor diet, obesity, smoking, heart problems, diabetes, alcohol consumption and psychosocial factors (such as stress or poor mental health).
High blood pressure alone accounted for almost half of the strokes that occurred in people aged 55 and under. Lack of regular exercise accounted for more than a third.

A UK study, which looked at 1,765 people aged 18-49 who were hospitalised for a stroke, found 42% of patients had high blood pressure, 24% high cholesterol, 23% smoked and 14% had diabetes. About 7% reported recreational drug use.
Rates of obesity and diabetes have been rising in younger people for three decades. These conditions, along with high blood pressure, are often undiagnosed or undertreated in younger adults.

But left untreated, these health problems can quietly raise stroke risk. For instance, research found that under-55s with diabetes were about 3.5 times as likely to suffer a stroke or mini-stroke than those who didn’t have the condition. Those with high blood pressure were about 2.5 times as likely.

But these factors don’t explain everything. Around half of strokes in young people that were caused by a blood clot had no clear cause. Research also shows a growing number of the strokes experienced by young people have no known risk factor.

Researchers are now investigating alternative risk factors, including air pollution, autoimmune conditions and illicit drug use. Stress and overworking are also increasingly being linked to higher risk of stroke in young people.

Lack of awareness is part of the problem, too, as my systematic review showed. People who don’t see themselves as at risk are less likely to visit their doctor or change their lifestyle. Alongside risk factors that already go undetected, this may partly explain why stroke rates in younger adults haven’t fallen as they have in older people.
The signs young people miss
Stroke in younger adults can be easier to miss as well.

A large US analysis found that people aged 18-44 were the age group most likely to be sent home from emergency departments with a missed stroke, often after complaining of dizziness or headache. A Stroke Association survey also found a quarter of stroke survivors aged 60 and under said they were initially misdiagnosed.

The signs of a stroke in younger people can sometimes be different than they are in older people. While most people will look out for symptoms such as face drooping on one side, arms that can’t both be lifted and speech that’s slurred or confused, young people don’t always fit this pattern.

Strokes at the back of the brain, which affects balance and vision rather than the face and arms, are more common in young adults. In these cases, symptoms can manifest as problems with balance or eyesight, a headache, neck pain or vertigo.

Not only can these symptoms be missed by healthcare workers, young people themselves may explain them away as a migraine, tiredness, a hangover or an inner ear problem. Symptoms can also stop after a short time. Even if they do, you should still get medical help immediately.
Speed matters. Clot-busting treatment generally has to be given within 4.5 hours of symptoms starting. The sooner it’s given, the better the outcome and recovery.
The good news is that most strokes in younger people are linked to things we can change.

The first thing you can do to lower your risk is to know your blood pressure. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so it’s important to have yours checked. You should also get checked for diabetes and high cholesterol, especially if you’re overweight or have a family history of heart disease or stroke.

Lifestyle matters, too. Don’t smoke, avoid recreational drugs and keep alcohol to no more than 14 units a week. It’s also recommended you eat less salt (no more than 6g a day) and more fibre, as these will help keep your blood pressure and cholesterol down.
Exercise is also key. Aim to get at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as fast walking or cycling.

You should also take stress and long working hours seriously. Both have been linked to a higher risk of stroke in their own right, even after accounting for other risk factors such as high blood pressure and smoking.
Stroke is no longer just an older person’s problem. Knowing the signs, and acting fast, could save your life or someone else’s.

David Olawade is a co-investigator on the Women’s Inclusion in Stroke Education and Readiness for Artificial Intelligence/Digital Technologies (WISER-AID) project, which is funded by the Burdett Trust for Nursing.

articles.title: I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense
articles.author: Adam Annaccone, Clinical Associate Professor of Kinesiology, University of Texas at Arlington
paras: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

That moment stayed with me. I’ve spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I’m a clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children’s athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages.

And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it’s easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I’m more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them.

As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I’ll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what’s appropriate as their children’s sports experiences intensify.

When I’m watching my children play, I’d rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I’m happy to help. They usually decide when we’re done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That’s fine too.
Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.

Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to make decisions about their participation.

As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn’t mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.

I’ve heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn’t always easy when your child is part of a team.

But more training doesn’t automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. Training places demands on the body, and athletes need time to adapt.

The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with increased overuse injury risk and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.

As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they’re experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn’t keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.

Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop coordination and a range of movement skills. The International Olympic Committee recommends varied physical activity and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize.

Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to want to continue participating, research shows. When young soccer players were asked what made sports fun, they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won’t accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.
Leaving the game at the field

In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn’t and what needs attention. But children don’t need a performance review every time they climb into the car.

I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I’ll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that’s fine too.

Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and sports came up relatively infrequently. They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don’t establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.

No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I’m comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I’m far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.
